title: SR&ED Specified Employees and Owner Salaries | Canada FAQ
description: Can you include owner salaries or specified employees in a Canadian SR&ED claim? Read our FAQ on wage caps, bonus rules, and R&D labour limits.
summary: Under Canada's SR&ED program, founders and specified employees—those owning 10% or more of any class of shares or not dealing at arm's length with the employer—face strict salary rules. Their bonuses and profit-based pay are excluded from SR&ED expenditures, taxable benefits are excluded from the proxy salary base, and under the proxy method their includable salary is capped at the lesser of 75% of salary or 2.5 times the YMPE.

Executive Overview and Macro-Fiscal Architecture of Canadian R&D Incentives

Canada operates one of the most mature and financially significant research and development tax incentive regimes in the industrialized world, anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) program. Administered jointly through legislative policy established by the Department of Finance Canada and operational enforcement executed by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), the SR&ED program functions as the primary fiscal mechanism for stimulating private-sector technological innovation across the country. During the fiscal cycle ending in March 2026, the CRA processed between 23,677 and 24,000 claims and allowed approximately $4.6 billion in federal Investment Tax Credits (ITCs), underscoring the program's central role in national industrial policy.

Between late 2024 and early 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most consequential structural overhaul in more than a decade. Following two phases of Department of Finance consultations initiated in early 2024 and subsequent legislative proposals introduced across Budget 2024 and Budget 2025, Parliament enacted Bill C-15, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Effective retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the Bill C-15 reforms fundamentally recalibrated the federal SR&ED framework by doubling the annual enhanced expenditure limit from $3 million to $6 million, expanding the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the historic $10 million–$50 million range to $15 million–$75 million, extending eligibility for the 35% enhanced credit rate to eligible Canadian public corporations, and restoring the eligibility of capital expenditures and capital lease costs that had been repealed since January 1, 2014. Concurrently, at the provincial level, Revenu Québec enacted a sweeping modernization effective for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, consolidating its legacy suite of fragmented R&D tax credits into the unified Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation, or CRIC), while British Columbia permanently enacted its 10% credit and aligned its expenditure threshold with the new $6 million federal cap in Budget 2026.

The structural design of Canada's R&D tax architecture relies on a dual-benefit statutory mechanism codified within the Income Tax Act (ITA), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.), and the Income Tax Regulations (ITR). Under the first pillar, taxpayers are permitted to pool allowable current and, for acquisitions after December 15, 2024, capital SR&ED expenditures under subsection 37(1) of the ITA, deducting them in full against current-year business income or carrying the pool balance forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future years. Under the second pillar, taxpayers earn an Investment Tax Credit pursuant to subsections 127(5) and 127(9) of the ITA, which directly reduces federal Part I tax payable and, for qualifying corporations under section 127.1, yields a direct cash refund.

A critical second-order implication of this dual-tier structure is that the net economic recovery of an SR&ED claim is highly sensitive to corporate structure, capitalization, and provincial jurisdiction. Because provincial R&D tax credits and direct government grants—such as funding from the National Research Council's Industrial Research Assistance Program (IRAP)—are legally categorized as "government assistance" under subsection 127(9), they grind down the federal qualified expenditure pool on a dollar-for-dollar basis prior to the application of the federal ITC rate. Furthermore, federal ITCs claimed in a given taxation year either reduce the subsection 37(1) deductible expenditure pool in the subsequent taxation year or are brought into taxable income under the recapture and income inclusion mechanics of the ITA. Consequently, optimizing R&D recovery requires precise mathematical coordination between federal and provincial tax schedules, overhead calculation elections, and capital asset deployment strategies.
Federal Statutory Framework and Legislative Amendments (Bill C-15)
Core Statutory Provisions of the Income Tax Act and Regulations

The legal authority governing federal SR&ED incentives is distributed across several interlocking provisions of the Income Tax Act and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations. The statutory architecture separates the technical definition of eligible scientific and technological work from the accounting rules governing expenditure pooling and tax credit computation.

cells: Defines "scientific research and experimental development" as a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis, encompassing basic research, applied research, experimental development, and eight enumerated categories of eligible support work, while explicitly excluding routine or commercial activities under paragraphs (e) to (k).

Establishes the cumulative expenditure pool for SR&ED carried on in Canada. Subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) captures current expenditures directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer. Pool balances may be deducted in the current year or carried forward indefinitely.

Stipulates that no amount may be deducted under subsection 37(1) in respect of an expenditure unless the taxpayer files the prescribed form (Form T661) containing prescribed information within 12 months after the taxpayer's filing-due date for the taxation year.
Investment Tax Credit (ITC) Calculation and Definitions

Governs the deduction of ITCs against Part I tax otherwise payable. Subsection 127(9) defines "qualified expenditure", "SR&ED qualified expenditure pool", and "expenditure limit", while paragraph (m) enforces the 12-month post-filing-due-date bar for ITC claims.

Provides the statutory mechanism through which qualifying Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and eligible Canadian public corporations receive cash refunds for unused ITCs earned during the taxation year.

Subsection 2900(4) establishes the notional overhead proxy rate at 55% of the directly engaged salary base. Subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) impose statutory ceilings on the inclusion of salaries paid to specified employees within the proxy base.

body.text: The Bill C-15 Modernization Package (Effective Post-December 15, 2024)

Enacted via Bill C-15 upon Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, the federal legislative amendments address long-standing structural criticisms that the SR&ED regime penalized domestic technology firms as they scaled past startup thresholds or accessed public equity markets. The reforms apply to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, with the capital expenditure and lease provisions applying to property acquired and becoming available for use, or lease costs incurred, after December 15, 2024.

The centrepiece of the Bill C-15 reform is the doubling of the maximum annual qualified expenditure limit eligible for the enhanced 35% federal ITC from $3,000,000 to $6,000,000. At the 35% statutory rate, a qualifying corporation can now generate up to $2,100,000 per year in fully refundable federal tax credits on current expenditures, compared to the previous ceiling of $1,050,000. Alongside this higher cap, Parliament expanded the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds. Under the legacy rules, a CCPC's $3,000,000 expenditure limit began phasing out once the taxable capital employed in Canada by the corporation and its associated corporate group in the preceding taxation year reached $10,000,000, and was completely eliminated at $50,000,000. (Historically, prior to the Federal Budget 2019 amendments effective for taxation years ending on or after April 2019, the expenditure limit was also ground down when prior-year taxable income fell between $500,000 and $800,000.) For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 raised the lower phase-out threshold to $15,000,000 and the upper elimination threshold to $75,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada, or average gross revenue if elected under the new public company rules.

In addition to expanding the expenditure cap and capital phase-out corridor, Bill C-15 eliminated the "IPO cliff" by extending the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to eligible Canadian public corporations. Historically, the moment a Canadian private technology or life-sciences firm executed an Initial Public Offering or became controlled by a public corporation, it ceased to qualify as a CCPC, causing its federal SR&ED rate to drop precipitously from a 35% refundable credit to a 15% non-refundable credit. Under the amended legislation, eligible Canadian public corporations—resident in Canada, not controlled by non-residents, and satisfying the revenue or taxable capital thresholds—enjoy access to the 35% refundable credit on up to $6,000,000 of annual qualified expenditures. Finally, reversing the 2012 federal budget measure that had eliminated capital expenditures from SR&ED eligibility effective January 1, 2014, Bill C-15 restored both the subsection 37(1) deduction and the section 127 ITC for qualifying depreciable property acquired and becoming available for use after December 15, 2024, as well as equipment lease expenditures incurred after that date.

body.text: Mathematical Mechanics of the Expenditure Limit Phase-Out

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the $6,000,000 annual expenditure limit must be allocated among all associated corporations within a corporate group. Where the combined taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation and its associated corporations in the immediately preceding taxation year exceeds $15,000,000, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced on a straight-line basis and reaches zero at $75,000,000. Expressed mathematically for a full 365-day taxation year, the annual Expenditure Limit is determined by:

where A represents the amount, up to a maximum of $60,000,000, by which the combined taxable capital employed in Canada of the claimant and all associated corporations for the preceding taxation year exceeds $15,000,000. Under this formula, every $10 of prior-year taxable capital above $15,000,000 reduces the enhanced expenditure limit by $1. By way of illustration, a mid-market manufacturing firm with $45,000,000 in prior-year taxable capital would have suffered an 87.5% reduction of its $3,000,000 limit under the legacy $10 million–$50 million rules, leaving an expenditure limit of only $375,000. Conversely, under the Bill C-15 formula, its expenditure limit is reduced by exactly 50% of $6,000,000, preserving a $3,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit eligible for the 35% refundable rate.
Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Overhead Elections, and Cloud Computing Rules
Salaries and Wages: Regular vs. Specified Employees

To enter the SR&ED expenditure pool on Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31, expenditures must fall within strictly defined statutory categories incurred for SR&ED carried on in Canada and related to a business of the claimant. Eligible labour costs consist of salaries and wages paid to employees who are directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, representing 60% to 80% of most claims. The CRA enforces a sharp legal distinction between regular arm's-length employees and "specified employees". A specified employee is defined as an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or who owns, directly or indirectly, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation.

For specified employees, bonuses and remuneration based on profits are excluded from SR&ED expenditures under subsection 37(9) of the ITA under both the proxy and traditional calculation methods, taxable benefits are excluded from the salary base used to compute the Prescribed Proxy Amount, and the CRA closely scrutinizes founder salaries that exceed fair market rates. Furthermore, when calculating the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) in Part 5 of Form T661 under ITR subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8), the includable salary of a specified employee is capped at the lesser of 75% of the employee's total salary (pro-rated for time spent on SR&ED) and 2.5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) under the Canada Pension Plan. Associated corporations employing the same specified employee must execute and file Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)) under subsections 37(9.1) to 37(9.5) of the ITA; otherwise, the specified employee's salary or wages are not SR&ED expenditures, and the total allocated among the associated corporations may not exceed 5 times the YMPE. Under the Proxy Method, only the portion of salaries and wages of employees who directly undertake, supervise, or support hands-on technical SR&ED work may be included in the salary base, whereas indirect administrative or clerical support is excluded.
Overhead and Other Expenditures: The Proxy Method vs. Traditional Method Election

At the outset of preparing Form T661 (Part 3, Section A), the claimant must make an annual, irrevocable election for the taxation year between the Proxy Method (elected on Line 160) and the Traditional Method (elected on Line 162). This election applies uniformly across all SR&ED projects claimed in that fiscal year, and taxpayers cannot retroactively switch methods once the return is filed.

body.text: Cloud Computing, AI Training Compute, and Software Subscriptions

A widespread compliance error in Canadian technology, software-as-a-service (SaaS), and data analytics SR&ED claims involves the improper classification of cloud computing infrastructure—such as Amazon Web Services (AWS), Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud Platform (GCP)—and software or API subscriptions. Although informal startup advisories occasionally group non-production staging and testing cloud environments under "materials consumed", authoritative CRA audit policy and statutory interpretation establish that cloud computing is an intangible utility or hosting service rather than a physical material consumed or transformed.

Consequently, cloud computing and software subscription costs cannot be claimed separately when a taxpayer elects the Proxy Method on Line 160. Because the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount legally substitutes for all overhead and other directly related expenditures, claiming cloud invoices alongside the 55% proxy results in automatic disallowance during CRA financial review. Conversely, under the Traditional Method (Line 162), cloud compute and third-party development API costs are fully claimable on Line 360 provided the taxpayer maintains strict accounting segregation between commercial production infrastructure (coded to Cost of Goods Sold) and dedicated R&D/experimental development infrastructure, and proves that the compute cycles were directly related and incremental to the SR&ED project.

This regulatory divergence creates a decisive mathematical trade-off for artificial intelligence, machine learning, and data-intensive companies. For a team of five engineers with $600,000 in eligible SR&ED salaries, electing the Proxy Method generates $330,000 in notional overhead. However, if that team incurs incremental cloud compute and GPU cluster expenses exceeding $330,000 to train experimental models, electing the Traditional Method yields a materially larger SR&ED claim on the exact same underlying technical work. Because a taxpayer cannot switch methods retroactively after seeing its year-end bills, compute-heavy enterprises must implement SR&ED-aware cloud resource tagging and project-level cost accounting from the first day of the fiscal year.
Materials Consumed or Transformed, Prototypes, and Production Runs

Eligible material costs encompass the cost of physical materials, including shipping costs to the claimant's facility, that are either consumed (rendered virtually valueless or turned into scrap during experiments) or transformed into another product or asset in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada. The CRA evaluates material and asset development claims under two primary administrative policies: the While Developing an Asset Policy and the Production Runs Policy.

Under the While Developing an Asset Policy, the CRA distinguishes between a pilot plant, a commercial plant, a prototype, and a custom commercial asset by examining how and why the asset was constructed and used. The design, construction, and testing of a prototype fall within basic research, applied research, or experimental development, and because a prototype ordinarily has no commercial application or only nominal scrap value once tested, the labour and material expenditures incurred to build it are treated as current expenditures wholly attributable to SR&ED. Where input materials form part of a prototype or pilot plant that retains commercial value after testing, they are treated as materials transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED, and subsequent sale or conversion to commercial use triggers recapture rules. Similarly, under the Production Runs Policy, when experimental development is conducted on a commercial manufacturing line, the claimant must establish through technical evidence whether the run constitutes Experimental Development with Experimental Production (ED+EP) or Experimental Development with Commercial Production (ED+CP). Any labour, overhead, or material costs attributable to commercial production or excess production volume are disallowed as SR&ED expenditures.
Subcontractors and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant engages an arm's-length Canadian subcontractor—defined as an individual with a valid Social Insurance Number or a corporation/registered business with a GST/HST Business Number—to perform SR&ED work on the claimant's behalf in Canada, 100% of the contract cost is deductible in the subsection 37(1) expenditure pool, but only 80% of the eligible contract amount enters the subsection 127(9) qualified expenditure pool to earn Investment Tax Credits. Any portion of subcontracted work performed offshore outside Canada is completely ineligible. In addition, in a contract SR&ED situation, the contract must confer ownership rights to the underlying SR&ED work to the payer at the time the work is performed. Where SR&ED contracts occur between persons not dealing at arm's length, the contract payment itself does not qualify for ITCs; rather, the performing corporation incurs the underlying expenditures and the parties may file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length, reported across Lines 508, 538, 540, and 544 of Form T661) alongside Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length).

Distinct from subcontractors performing bespoke work on the claimant's behalf are Third-Party Payments, governed by the CRA's Third-Party Payments Policy and reported on Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)). Third-party payments are monetary contributions made to five classes of approved entities (Entities A through E, comprising Canadian resident corporations for basic or applied research, approved associations, approved universities, colleges, or research institutes, non-profit SR&ED corporations, and agricultural organizations funded via producer check-off dues). For a third-party payment to qualify, the funds must be used for SR&ED carried on in Canada, the SR&ED must be related to a business of the claimant, and the claimant must be legally entitled to exploit the results of that SR&ED in its business as a direct consequence of the payment. Eligible third-party payments are included in qualified expenditures at the 80% inclusion rate.
Capital Expenditures and Lease Costs (Restored Post-December 15, 2024)

Under the Bill C-15 legislative restoration, depreciable property acquired and becoming available for use after December 15, 2024 qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure if the claimant intended, in the year claimed and over the asset's expected useful life, either to use all or substantially all (ASA)—defined as 90% or more—of the operating time in its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or to consume ASA (90% or more) of its value to perform SR&ED in Canada. Non-depreciable assets such as land, as well as buildings and leasehold interests in buildings, are statutorily excluded from SR&ED capital eligibility.

Taxpayers claiming restored capital expenditures must navigate specific accounting rules on Form T661. Capital expenditures claimed on Line 390 enter the subsection 37(1) pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and therefore must not be included on Schedule T2SCH8 for regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) depreciation. Crucially, while expenditures for used depreciable equipment satisfying the 90% ASA test are entered on Line 390 and enter the deductible SR&ED expenditure pool, used equipment does not qualify for the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit; only new depreciable property earns the section 127 ITC. Furthermore, if SR&ED capital property is subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, both SR&ED ITC recapture and CCA recapture rules may be triggered. For equipment leases, lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for property used 90% or more in SR&ED qualify directly as SR&ED lease expenditures (provided the underlying depreciable property was acquired after December 15, 2024), whereas claimants using the Traditional Method may claim lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 for equipment used less than 90% of the time in SR&ED on Line 360 as overhead and other expenditures.
Jurisprudential Foundation and CRA Technical Eligibility Criteria
The Statutory Definition and the Five-Question Judicial Standard

Whether a technical project constitutes eligible SR&ED is a mixed question of fact and law governed by subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act. The statute defines SR&ED as a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis, encompassing three primary branches: basic research (work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, such as theoretical and experimental particle physics), applied research (work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view), and experimental development (work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes).

When a core basic, applied, or experimental development project is established in Canada, subsection 248(1) also admits Support Work where it is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the core research or experimental development, strictly limited to eight enumerated categories: engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, and psychological research. Conversely, paragraphs (e) through (k) of subsection 248(1) explicitly exclude market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities; prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection.

The authoritative judicial framework for determining whether an activity satisfies subsection 248(1) was established by Judge Bowman in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520 (TCC), and formally adopted by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393 (at paragraph 17). Canadian courts evaluate five sequential criteria across all SR&ED appeals:

body.text: Administrative Guidelines vs. Recent Tax Court Jurisprudence

In 2021, the CRA replaced its archived Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy (2012/2015) with the updated Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives. Administratively, the CRA structures its technical review around a two-step inquiry—first determining whether SR&ED exists via the five questions, and second determining the extent of eligible work including support work and excluded activities—which is frequently summarized for claimants as a three-question test focusing on Technological Uncertainty, Systematic Investigation, and Technological Advancement.

In recent Tax Court of Canada jurisprudence, judges have closely scrutinized overly restrictive administrative interpretations by the CRA, as demonstrated in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2025 TCC, Justice Sommerfeldt), following earlier judicial analyses in Novalia Power General Research Inc. v. The Queen (2016 TCC) and R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. The Queen (2015 TCC). In Manning Canning, the appellant attempted to develop a cold-pressed juice beverage capable of remaining shelf-stable at room temperature for at least two years without conventional thermal pasteurization or refrigeration. The Minister of National Revenue disallowed the claim, arguing that refrigeration was a well-known routine method for inhibiting yeast, bacteria, and mould growth, and that the appellant had merely carried on routine product development using non-scientific procedures.

Justice Sommerfeldt rejected the Minister's characterization and allowed the taxpayer's appeal on a balance of probabilities. The Court held that testing the natural preservative Chiber outside of its known dairy application within a cold-pressed juice matrix did not constitute routine engineering because standard procedures failed to yield predictable results, thereby establishing genuine technological uncertainty followed by hypothesis formulation and experimental trials. Equally important, Justice Sommerfeldt clarified the fifth C.W. Agencies criterion regarding documentation, ruling that while contemporaneous records may be necessary to resolve factual disputes between the parties, "the existence of contemporaneous documentation, or contemporaneous documents with specific intent, is not a condition to the recognition of scientific research or experimental development". Notwithstanding this vital judicial protection at the Tax Court level, claimants undergoing administrative CRA reviews by Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) are strongly advised to maintain contemporaneous engineering artifacts—including Git commit histories, Jira or Asana task tags, architecture decision records, sprint logs, and dated experimental test logs—to prevent costly audit disputes.
Governing Authorities, Filing Procedures, Deadlines, and Audit Defence
Institutional Division of Labour and Prescribed Tax Forms

The administration of the federal SR&ED regime is divided between the Department of Finance Canada, which exercises authority over tax policy and legislative drafting, and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which administers compliance through a dedicated SR&ED Directorate. When a claim is selected for review by the CRA, evaluation is bifurcated between a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA), who examines the technical narrative in Part 2 of Form T661 and conducts technical interviews with the claimant's lead engineers or scientists, and a Financial Reviewer (FR), who verifies general ledger accounts, T4 payroll summaries, subcontractor invoices, proof of payment, and Schedule T2SCH31 calculations.
To submit a valid federal SR&ED claim, taxpayers must file the prescribed forms with their annual income tax return.

body.text: The Absolute 18-Month Statutory Filing Deadline and Pre-Claim Approval

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant must file Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) identifying all qualified expenditures no later than 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year. Because a corporation's T2 return filing-due date is 6 months after its fiscal year-end, a corporate claimant has a maximum of 18 months after the end of its fiscal year to file its SR&ED claim (for example, a December 31, 2024 fiscal year-end has a T2 due date of June 30, 2025, and an absolute SR&ED filing deadline of June 30, 2026). This 18-month reporting deadline is an absolute statutory requirement with no ministerial discretion or administrative mechanism to grant an extension; missing the deadline by a single day permanently bars the claim.

To provide upfront technical certainty prior to tax filing, the CRA introduced an optional Pre-Claim Approval process (operational since April 2026), which allows claimants to obtain formal confirmation of technical project eligibility within an administrative target of 90 days before submitting their T2 corporate tax return. Once the T2 return and Form T661 are filed, the CRA generally processes unreviewed refundable claims within 60 to 120 days, whereas first-time, complex, or audited claims undergoing RTA and FR review typically require 120 to 180 days. While claimants may prepare filings in-house or utilize automated documentation platforms, external SR&ED consultants commonly charge contingency fees ranging from 15% to 25% of the approved credit, though the legal responsibility for ensuring a compliant claim rests strictly on the signing taxpayer.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes

Nearly all Canadian provinces supplement the federal SR&ED program with provincial R&D tax incentives. Outside of Quebec (where claims are filed with Revenu Québec alongside the CO-17 corporate return) and Alberta (where the Innovation Employment Grant is claimed through the Alberta Corporate Income Tax Return), provincial R&D credits are harmonized with the federal definition of SR&ED under subsection 248(1) and are collected via provincial schedules attached to the federal T2 return.

body.text: Deep Dive: Quebec's 2025/2026 CRIC Overhaul

Historically, Quebec operated a multi-layered set of R&D tax credits administered by Revenu Québec. Pursuant to the Quebec 2025–2026 Budget and Revenu Québec's administrative guidance issued on July 9, 2025, the province unified its innovation tax system for taxation years or fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025 by creating the Tax Credit for R&D, Innovation and Pre-Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation – CRIC).

To achieve this unification, Quebec abolished six legacy incentives: the R&D salary and subcontractor credit, the credit for university research or public research centres, the credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium, the credit for pre-competitive research in private partnership, the credit for technological adaptation services, and the industrial design component of the design tax credit, while simultaneously abolishing the personal income tax holiday for foreign researchers and foreign experts. Under the new regime, eligible corporations claim the CRIC on Form RD-1029.8.CR (entering code 112 for the R&D component and code 113 for the pre-commercialization component on lines 440p to 440y of the CO-17 return), accompanied by Form RD-222 for the deduction of R&D expenditures, Form RD-1029.8.EN to allocate the $1,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit among associated corporations, and Form RD-1029.8.PR to report pre-commercialization activities.

The CRIC introduces three major structural shifts for Quebec innovators. First, it extends refundable tax credit coverage beyond strict R&D to encompass pre-commercialization work performed in continuity with R&D—such as product testing, technological validation, and prototyping—as well as qualifying capital expenditures on property used in R&D and pre-commercialization (complementing Quebec's separate C3i Tax Credit for Investment and Innovation on Form CO-1029.8.36.II, which offers up to 25% for eligible equipment). Second, the CRIC replaces the old bi-level salary exclusion threshold with a modified exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 (pro-rated for the number of days in the taxation year) or the sum of the employee-specific thresholds calculated from the basic personal tax amount for employees engaged in R&D and pre-commercialization. Third, once net eligible expenditures exceed this exclusion threshold, the CRIC provides a 100% refundable tax credit at a rate of 30% on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures, and 20% on all eligible expenditures beyond $1,000,000 (with corporate members of a partnership receiving the flat 20% refundable rate without access to the 30% tier).
Financial Modelling, Government Assistance Grinding, and Combined Recovery
Interaction of Provincial Credits, IRAP Grants, and the Federal Pool

Under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, any government assistance or non-government assistance that a taxpayer receives, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of SR&ED reduces the qualified expenditure pool prior to computing the federal Investment Tax Credit. Consequently, direct R&D grants—such as NRC IRAP contributions—cannot be claimed simultaneously for SR&ED on the same dollar of expenditure; the IRAP-funded portion is deducted from the SR&ED expenditure base. Similarly, provincial R&D tax credits (including Ontario's OITC and ORDTC, British Columbia's SR&ED credit, Alberta's IEG, and the R&D component of Quebec's CRIC) constitute government assistance that reduces the federal qualified expenditure pool in the year claimed.

For a qualifying CCPC claiming within the $6,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit in a province where the provincial credit rate applies to the eligible expenditure base (net of direct grants), the combined federal and provincial tax credit recovery is expressed by:
Combined Recovery = Provincial Credit + 35% × (Eligible Expenditures + PPA − Provincial Credit)

where PPA represents the federal Prescribed Proxy Amount on directly engaged salaries. In the taxation year following receipt or application of the federal ITC, the federal credit reduces the corporation's subsection 37(1) SR&ED deductible expenditure pool or is included in corporate taxable income.
Worked Numerical Case Study: Post-Bill C-15 CCPC Claim

Consider a qualifying CCPC operating in Ontario during its fiscal year beginning January 1, 2025, with prior-year taxable capital below $15,000,000 and prior-year taxable income below $500,000, entitling it to the full $6,000,000 federal enhanced limit and the full $3,000,000 Ontario OITC limit. During the year, the corporation incurs $430,000 in eligible salaries for employees directly engaged in SR&ED and $142,500 in eligible arm's-length Canadian subcontractor invoices, and elects the Proxy Method on Line 160 of Form T661.

Strategic Conclusions and Audit Risk Mitigation Framework

The enactment of Bill C-15 at the federal level and the introduction of the CRIC in Quebec represent a paradigm shift in Canadian innovation tax policy. By doubling the federal enhanced expenditure cap to $6,000,000, stretching the taxable capital phase-out corridor to $15,000,000–$75,000,000, admitting eligible Canadian public corporations to the 35% refundable credit tier, and restoring capital expenditure eligibility for acquisitions after December 15, 2024, Parliament has removed the structural disincentives that previously constrained scaling Canadian technology and manufacturing enterprises. At the same time, the CRA's deployment of advanced data analytics and rigorous joint reviews by Research and Technology Advisors and Financial Reviewers demands heightened governance across corporate tax and engineering functions.

To maximize refundable recoveries while insulating claims from audit adjustments, corporations should institutionalize rigorous internal controls at the start of each fiscal year. First, finance and engineering leaders in compute-intensive sectors must perform an upfront mathematical comparison between the 55% Proxy Method (Line 160) and the Traditional Method (Line 162) rather than defaulting blindly to the proxy election; where incremental non-production cloud computing (AWS, GCP, Azure) and partial-use equipment leases exceed 55% of the directly engaged salary base, electing the Traditional Method and maintaining resource-tagged R&D cloud accounts from Day 1 unlocks substantial additional credits and avoids proxy-method disallowances. Second, capital asset procurement teams must document both the post-December 15, 2024 "available for use" date and operational time logs verifying the 90% all-or-substantially-all SR&ED usage threshold over the equipment's expected useful life, while ensuring used equipment is segregated from ITC calculations and all Line 390 capital assets are excluded from Schedule T2SCH8 CCA claims. Finally, claimants should integrate contemporaneous hypothesis tracking directly into version control and project management tools, utilize the CRA's 90-day Pre-Claim Approval pathway for novel projects, restructuring Quebec accounting charts to capture post-March 25, 2025 pre-commercialization costs under the CRIC, and enforce strict internal filing calendars well ahead of the unextendable 18-month statutory deadline under subsections 37(11) and 127(9)(m).
